title.narrative: Output 7.1. Increased capacity of Member States to ensure respect for, promote and realize fundamental principles and rights at work

description.narrative: In 2023, the Government of Malawi adopted a national action plan to tackle child labour, considering the dangers of the erosion of Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (FPRW) due to the COVID-19 crisis. This follows a national meeting that was held in 2022 to devise an action plan to address child labour in Malawi. The roadmap supports the Implementation of Malawi's national Alliance 8.7 Pathfinder Country status that calls for enhanced commitment and collaboration from all stakeholders, in finding traditional and innovative financing instruments to support the achievement SDG target 8.7 (child labour, worst forms of child labour, forced labour, human trafficking and modern slavery). The roadmap is yet to be validated. The national action plan sets out clear priorities and areas of interventions for Malawi to achieve SDG Target 8.7 during the period 2022 - 2025, articulates strategic outcomes, specifies timelines, sets annual benchmarks and indicators to measure progress, clearly defines roles and responsibilities, and identifies resources required and any resource gaps, within the framework of Alliance 8.7, and in line with Malawi’s status as a Pathfinder Country In September 2022, ILO convened a national strategic planning meeting to discuss the development of a national action plan for the elimination of Child labour in Malawi. The ILO provided inputs into the draft action plan which were incorporated in the final plan approved by the Government. Another meeting was held in February 2023 to review feedback from stakeholders including the ILO which was also incorporated into the final document. Prior to this, ILO had conducted a study on the Tenancy system in Malawi and its link to child labour in the country. The study also informed the formulation of the national Action plan on elimination of Child labour. Another survey ILO conducted was on the prevalence of child labour in global supply chains. In 2022 A Child labour survey in the tea and coffee sector was conducted following the reported gap of the 2015 National child labour survey that did not have sector specific information on the prevalence of child labour. Therefore, the ILO in 2022 conducted a survey on the prevalence on the child labour in the tea and coffee supply chain where in November and December of 2022. This report also informed the formulation of the National Action Plan on the elimination of child labour.

description.narrative: In the context of the implementation of the 2021 law abolishing the tenancy system, the Government of Malawi, together with social partners, introduced several initiatives to advance decent working conditions and labour rights in the tobacco and tea sectors. The National Statistics Office's capacity has been enhanced to collect data on tenancy labour and child labour. The Tobacco and Allied Workers Union of Malawi (TOAWUM) has been reinvigorated and the strengthening of its membership base, which reached 7,000 members, has been supported. Furthermore, community-level social dialogue structures and cooperatives have been established and capacitated in the targeted districts. To empower women and promote gender equality, women have been supported in taking key leadership positions in these social dialogue committees. A comprehensive campaign has been launched across various media platforms to inform the public about the abolition of the tenancy labour system and the importance of ensuring decent work, starting with fundamental rights, including the right of children to be free from child labour. The Ministry of Labour, together with social partners developed and piloted a Workplace Self-Monitoring Guide to support enterprises’ capacity to comply with national laws and international labour standards. Members of the Employers' Consultative Association of Malawi (ECAM) have been trained on international labour standards, with a focus on forced labour, the abolition of the tenancy system, and the prevention of workplace violence and harassment. A strategic compliance planning session was held in September 2022 for 35 government offices (25 men and 10 women), including labour inspectors, with a specific emphasis on tobacco, tea, and coffee supply chains, to strengthen labour inspection within their respective districts. The Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) has been promoted and incorporated into all training programs conducted under two ILO projects. In April 2022, the ILO, with support from the Royal Norwegian embassy, provided technical support to follow up with the government's amendment of the Employment Act aimed at abolishing the tenancy labour system. A national meeting that brought together key stakeholders from various sectors was organized and a plan towards gradual phasing out of the tenancy labour system was developed. The ILO conducted a legislative gap analysis, which was presented to the constituents in September 2023. The ILO also provided support to the Ministry of Labour in the development of a Workplace Self-monitoring Guide to support enterprises’ efforts to comply with national laws and adhere to international labour standards. In June 2022, the ILO convened a national meeting with the Malawi Congress of Trade Unions and the International Union of Food, Agricultural, Hotel, Restaurant, Catering, Tobacco and Allied Workers’ Associations (IUF) to discuss measures to address decent work deficits in the Tobacco sector. The meeting agreed to develop and launch an Advocacy and Communications Strategy on Child labour with ILO technical support which has been approved and launched. Efforts to revamp the TOAWUM have been supported and community-level social dialogue structures were set up. A campaign was launched to raise awareness among the public about the abolition of the tenancy system and the importance of ensuring access to decent work, staring with the respect for fundamental principles and rights at work. Convention 190 has been promoted and issues related to violence and harassment at work have been mainstreamed in all ADDRESS and ACCEL project activities.
